synthesis.headline: Western upper low ejects into Canada, firing northern-Plains storms while the southern heat dome digs in and the meridional regime regenerates poleward rather than flattening
synthesis.narrative:
The organizing story is the same three-part arrangement Tlaloc has tracked all week, but with the western piece now on the move. The deep, positively tilted longwave trough that had been anchored offshore has closed off near the British Columbia/Washington border and is ejecting northeast; its parent surface low is tracking into southern Saskatchewan, dragging a cold front down into the northern Plains and upper Midwest. That leaves the day's dividing line running from the Canadian Prairies into the Dakotas. To its south, the amplified central ridge (heights near 594 dam over Oklahoma/Kansas) keeps the south-central US baking, and along the Gulf and Southeast a moist tropical airmass sits under a stalled, weak front. In short: the western trough is finally lifting out rather than sitting still, but the southern heat and the Southeast moisture regime are unmoved.

Today's centers of action are all on the ridge periphery, not in the deep Plains. The best-organized severe threat is the SPC slight-risk corridor across the north-central and northeast Plains, where afternoon redevelopment along a dryline-like surface trough and pre-frontal trough favors supercells with large hail as the primary hazard; a secondary tornado risk is flagged over southeast South Dakota where low-level shear is strongest. Heavy rain is the co-threat on the trough's cool side, with a slight excessive-rainfall risk in northwestern Montana today and the axis shifting to Iowa Tuesday into early Wednesday as the front advances. Along the central Gulf Coast, a hot, moist airmass ahead of the weak front supports intense pulse storms with damaging downbursts through the afternoon. Under the ridge, the durable signal persists — heat indices of 105-110 degrees and record-warm overnight lows across the midsection — while the West runs 10-25 degrees below normal with freezing mornings possible at higher elevations behind the departing low. Offshore, the East Pacific remains busy while the Atlantic stays quiet.

Aloft, the 500 mb pattern remains firmly meridional. The tight height gradient on the northern flank of the western trough, from the Pacific Northwest into the northern Rockies, marks a concentrated 70-100 kt jet corridor — that is the dynamical support ejecting the surface low into Canada and driving the northern-Plains convection. The Air Mass RGB shows a broad red-orange dry swath over the central and southern Plains, low-PV subsidence air under the late-summer ridge (not a stratospheric intrusion given its size), which is the real reason the midsection heat holds — midlevel warming, subsidence, and capping — rather than any modest surface high. The more compact, cyclonically curved dry streamer over the southern Rockies and northern Mexico is a more credible stratospheric-intrusion signature, wrapping a weak trough/cutoff in that corner. The key evolution question is whether this meridional regime is breaking down, and the ensemble pair says no: at 6-10 days the positive height anomaly has relinquished its mid-latitude western grip (near-zero to slightly negative across the western CONUS) and consolidated poleward into a strong ridge over the Canadian Arctic, but by 8-14 days a positive anomaly rebuilds over western Canada and the northern Plains and the western CONUS trends weakly positive again. That is not a ridge that keeps shrinking; it is a meridional regime that regenerates, with recurring Northwest troughs punching through — the WPC extended discussion has exactly this, another closed low digging toward British Columbia by next weekend. Both the 6-10 and 8-14 charts keep a positive anomaly over the Southeast, and both keep the amplitude high. This breaks somewhat from yesterday's read of a collapsing high-latitude ridge: today's guidance amplifies the Arctic ridge instead. The takeaway is geographic relocation and poleward amplification — the ridge core sitting north and its heat anchor clinging to the southern tier — not a transition to zonal flow.
synthesis.climate_context: The ENSO table shows a strong El Niño in place, with the ONI reaching roughly +1.80 by summer 2026 after a steady, reversal-free warming trend from last winter's weak La Niña. The tropics are behaving accordingly: a hyperactive East Pacific carries Hurricane Lowell southwest of Hawaii, Tropical Storm Marie west of Baja, and a disturbance off southwestern Mexico with a 50 percent chance of development in seven days, set against a completely suppressed Atlantic where NHC expects no development for a week — a classic El Niño split at what is climatologically the Atlantic season's peak. The North American Monsoon remains active, feeding continued moisture and convection across the Southwest and southern Rockies into Mexico. Severe weather continues to express itself in its expected late-summer mode — ridge-periphery and frontal storms across the northern Plains and Southeast rather than deep-Plains outbreaks — while the most durable domestic signal remains the entrenched south-central US heat, which WPC expects to linger with Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk and record temperatures through much of the week.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and none in the past six hours. Watch the north-central/northeast Plains for supercells with large hail, and specifically southeast South Dakota for the secondary tornado threat where low-level shear is strongest. Flash-flood sensitivity runs with a slight excessive-rainfall risk in northwestern Montana today, shifting to Iowa Tuesday into early Wednesday. Damaging downbursts are the main story along the central Gulf Coast from mid-afternoon. In the West, freezing morning temperatures at higher elevations are notable this early in September. In Canada, the maturing cyclone is now the driver, tracking into southern Saskatchewan with a moderate post-frontal gradient beneath the interior BC/Yukon high; over Mexico, monsoonal convection continues over the southern Rockies and interior, with the curved dry streamer marking a weak cutoff in the southern Rockies/northern Mexico corner.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The most prominent features are a 1017 mb high over the Gulf of Alaska and a low of approximately 1042 mb labeled over the northern Rockies/northern Plains border region, though that reading seems unusually deep for September and may reflect a misread label — it appears to be the remnant or inverted trough area rather than a closed cyclone of that intensity, so treat the central pressure as uncertain. A cold front extends southward from a low near the Canadian border into the central Plains, with a second cold front segment apparent across the Upper Midwest, and a warm front appears to trail eastward toward the Great Lakes region; these boundaries together mark the primary zone of frontal lift across the north-central United States. Pressure gradients are tightest across the Pacific Northwest, where isobars are notably compressed between the offshore high and the inland low, implying the strongest surface wind forcing on the chart, while gradients are quite slack across the Southeast and Gulf Coast states where isobars are widely spaced. The surface moisture focus is most evident across the Gulf Coast and lower Mississippi Valley, where dewpoints in the low-to-mid 70s°F are visible alongside a surface trough and frontal boundaries that would concentrate low-level convergence and instability, particularly from eastern Texas into the Tennessee Valley. A secondary moisture and lift focus exists near the cold front crossing the central Plains, where the frontal boundary is interacting with Gulf moisture return on its eastern flank.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 00Z Monday 07 September 2026 shows a broad low pressure complex dominating the North Pacific east of the date line, with the deepest center near 988 mb positioned well offshore, and a trailing cold front sweeping southeastward into the continental interior. Over Canada, the most consequential feature is a cold front extending from a low near 1001 mb that appears to be situated over the northern prairies or southern Northwest Territories based on its position relative to the visible coastline geometry, with the frontal boundary pushing into the northern Great Plains and connecting to a series of lows over the central United States. A high of 1025 mb is centered over what appears to be the interior of British Columbia or southern Yukon, producing a moderate gradient between it and the low to its northeast, suggesting active post-frontal flow across the BC interior and Alberta foothills. Over the Canadian Arctic — well into the upper portion of the frame consistent with the polar projection — there are several lows in the 994 to 1000 mb range that would be unremarkable for that latitude and season. The eastern Canadian seaboard shows relatively slack pressure with a broad high around 1020 mb to the south, implying limited synoptic forcing over Quebec and the Maritimes at this analysis time.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a deep, positively tilted longwave trough centered over the Pacific Northwest, with a closed 500 mb low near the British Columbia/Washington border area. The closed contour — reading near 570 dam — confirms this is a genuine cutoff or near-cutoff low, self-contained from the broader westerlies rather than an open shortwave. An amplified ridge axis is evident across the central Rockies and High Plains, with heights climbing to near 594 dam over the Oklahoma/Kansas region where the high center (H) is marked, creating a large-amplitude western trough to central ridge dipole. The height gradient is tight along the northern flank of the trough from the Pacific Northwest into the northern Rockies, implying a concentrated jet corridor there, likely in the 70-100 knot range based on the contour spacing, though wind speed is inferred from geometry rather than plotted barbs. The overall pattern is retrogressive or at minimum weakly progressive: the blocked ridge over the central plains and the anchored closed low to the west suggest little downstream translation, consistent with a quasi-stationary large-scale regime rather than a zonal, progressive flow.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 07 Sep 2026 at 1331Z shows a broad swath of red-orange tones across the central and southern Plains into the mid-Mississippi Valley, consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under what is likely a sprawling late-summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion, given the areal extent and positioning. A sharper, more elongated orange-to-green color gradient runs roughly from the upper Midwest southeastward through the Ohio Valley toward the mid-Atlantic coast, marking the likely jet corridor implied by that airmass boundary, with drier air to the west-northwest and moister green tones to the east and south. Deep convection is visible as bright white, cold-topped clusters along and just inland of the Gulf Coast from roughly the Louisiana-Mississippi coast eastward into the Florida Panhandle and along the Florida peninsula, with additional isolated cells over the western Caribbean and southern Mexico. A secondary elongated dry streamer with more saturated orange tones is apparent over the southern Rockies and northern Mexico, curving cyclonically around what appears to be a trough or weak cutoff feature over that region, making it a more credible candidate for a stratospheric intrusion signature given its compact, curved geometry on the cyclonic side of the flow. The green moisture plume is deepest across the Southeast and Gulf of Mexico, consistent with a sustained tropical airmass feeding the scattered deep convection in that sector.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: At 1310Z on 7 September 2026, the full-disk Air Mass RGB shows a broad green swath across the tropics from the eastern Pacific through Central America, the Caribbean, and into the western Amazon basin, consistent with deep tropical moisture; several clusters of bright white high-topped convection are embedded along this belt, most notably over southern Mexico, the Caribbean arc, and the western Colombian/Ecuadorian coast. A sharp color transition from green to orange-red is visible across the southern United States and northern Mexico, marking the poleward edge of the tropical airmass and implying a frontal or subtropical boundary in that corridor. Over southern South America, a vigorous baroclinic system is evident near the southern tip of the continent, with a curved swath of white cloud wrapping into a deep blue-purple cold airmass centered over the far southern Atlantic, characteristic of a mature extratropical cyclone in the Southern Hemisphere westerlies. Across Canada and into the Arctic along the upper portion of the disk, alternating bands of blue-purple and orange-red suggest a wavy upper-level pattern with at least two trough-ridge couplets; a compact, elongated orange-red feature on the eastern Canadian flank of one trough is a plausible stratospheric-intrusion signature given its position on the cyclonic side of the flow, though the disk geometry makes precise placement uncertain. The eastern Pacific basin shows no well-organized tropical convective clusters at this time.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant signal on this chart is a broad above-normal temperature probability covering the southern tier from the Desert Southwest through Texas and the Gulf Coast states into the entire Southeast and mid-Atlantic, with the highest probabilities, in the 80-90 and 90-100 percent range, concentrated over southern Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. This core of very high confidence above-normal temperatures suggests a strongly persistent warm pattern at the surface, consistent with an upper-level ridge anchored over the south-central and southeastern United States through the September 12-16 window. A below-normal signal, in the 40-50 percent leaning-below range, sits over northern Montana and the Dakotas, indicating only a modest cool tilt rather than a strong cold signal. Much of the interior West, Great Plains, and Midwest falls in the 33-50 percent above-normal range, reflecting a weaker warm lean that grades northward into near-normal territory across the Pacific Northwest, the Rockies, and the Northeast. The sharp gradient from the near-normal and below-normal signal in the northern tier to the very high confidence above-normal signal in the South implies the outlook favors continuation of a split pattern, with below-normal heights in the northern latitudes and persistent ridging to the south, rather than a wholesale breakdown of the current regime.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 12-16 September 2026. The dominant feature is a deep, positively amplified pattern over the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Canada, where a closed high centered near the Canadian Arctic Archipelago corresponds to heights around 528-534 dam; the positive anomaly there reads near +90 dam on the dashed blue contours — that figure is implausible for a mid-tropospheric anomaly (normal range is single to low double digits in dam), so the dashed contours are almost certainly plotted in meters, making the core anomaly approximately +9 dam, which is a strong but physically reasonable warm ridge. Across the conterminous western United States and into the eastern Pacific, the anomaly contours show values near zero or slightly negative (the zero line appears to cut across roughly the Pacific Northwest into the central Plains), indicating the positive height anomaly that was likely present earlier has retreated northward into Canada and is not holding over western North America proper. A broad ridge axis is implied by the tightly packed, poleward-bowing height contours stretching from the Canadian Rockies northeast toward Baffin Island, while a weak trough axis is suggested by the modest height falls and slight negative anomalies across the central and eastern United States, where heights near 582-588 dam prevail. The overall pattern does not appear to be trending toward zonality — the meridional amplitude remains pronounced over Canada — but the ridge's center of action has shifted well into the high Arctic rather than being anchored over the western contiguous states, consistent with a pattern that has amplified poleward while relinquishing its grip on mid-latitudes.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb heights and anomalies (departures from normal) prognostic valid 14-20 September 2026, made 06 September 2026, with solid green contours showing heights at 60 dam intervals and dashed red/purple contours showing anomalies. The dominant feature is a strongly amplified ridge centered over the Canadian Arctic, with heights near 590 dam over the central Arctic and the ridge axis extending southward through the Canadian interior; western Canada including British Columbia, Alberta, and the northern Rockies shows heights around 576-582 dam, placing a positive height anomaly clearly over that region rather than retreated to the southwest. The positive anomaly contours (dashed red, reading roughly +20 to +30 dam — though I'd note that if those dashed lines are in meters rather than dam, the actual departures would be a more plausible +2 to +3 dam) extend from the Arctic southward through western Canada and into the northern Plains, consistent with well-above-normal heights across that entire corridor. A trough axis is implied by the sharp height gradient and packing of contours across the eastern two-thirds of Canada and into the Great Lakes region, where heights fall to near 546-552 dam. The southeastern United States shows positive anomaly contours as well, with heights near 582-588 dam over the Gulf Coast states, while the western contiguous US from the Pacific Coast inland appears relatively neutral to weakly positive.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Deep upper-level low ejecting from northern Rockies toward southern Canada drives strong to severe thunderstorms across northern Rockies and northern Plains today, with slight risk excessive rainfall in northwestern Montana. Cold front extends into upper Midwest tonight, with additional strong storms developing Tuesday across north-central Plains advancing to upper Midwest Wednesday. Slight risk excessive rainfall highlighted for Iowa Tuesday to early Wednesday. High-pressure system expands eastward bringing cooler weather to Northeast and Mid-Atlantic with highs mid-70s to low-80s; scattered thunderstorms persist Southeast as frontal boundary stalls. Heat dome continues over midsection with heat indices 105-110 degrees and record warm overnight temperatures through early week. Below-normal temperatures 10-25 degrees expand across West with freezing morning temperatures possible across higher elevations.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Deep upper trough over western CONUS with embedded shortwaves progressing northeast. Surface low tracking into southern Saskatchewan. Morning convection ongoing from central Montana into western North Dakota will shift northeast. Afternoon redevelopment expected along dryline-like surface trough from Saskatchewan low to western South Dakota low, and along pre-frontal trough from south-central South Dakota into northeast Colorado. Supercell potential with large hail primary hazard; tornado risk secondary, especially over southeast South Dakota with strong low-level wind shear. Isolated to widely scattered coverage due to lingering convective inhibition. Central Gulf Coast: hot, moist air mass ahead of weak front; intense pulse storms possible with damaging downbursts from mid-afternoon onward. Slight risk area: north-central/northeast Plains.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No organized convective threat is currently being actively monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Hurricane Lowell is several hundred miles southwest of Hawaii under active advisories. Tropical Storm Marie is several hundred miles west-southwest of Punta Eugenia, Mexico, also under advisories. A disorganized low-pressure trough several hundred miles south-southwest of southwestern Mexico shows gradual development potential, with 10 percent formation chance through 48 hours and 50 percent through 7 days. The system moves west-northwestward at 10-15 mph.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI values show a transition from weak La Niña conditions (NDJ 2025 at -0.60) toward El Niño through early 2026. Anomalies warm progressively, crossing into El Niño territory by spring 2026 (MAM at +0.46). By summer 2026, anomalies reach +1.80, indicating strong El Niño development. The trend is consistently warming with no reversals, suggesting confidence in El Niño establishment by mid-year.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains weakly negative (latest -0.34, 7-day mean -0.58), showing little change over the past week and favoring slight eastern troughing. AO oscillated sharply mid-period but returned to positive (+0.53 latest, 7-day near zero), offering minimal support for high-latitude blocking. NAO has strengthened its negative trend, falling to -1.01 on the 7-day mean (currently -0.66), suggesting conditions may favor cutoff lows becoming trapped over the Atlantic rather than escaping downstream. Note: summer teleconnections are weak; these indices provide directional context only.
